The source dates the Athenian plague 'between 430 and 410 BC'. The primary morphology paper (Bolhuis et al., 'Morphological and Structural Aspects of the Extremely Halophilic Archaeon Haloquadratum walsbyi', PMC3084702) describes flat square cells joined in fragile postage-stamp sheets, not fixed quartets; the genus name refers to the square cell shape. The local page says electron emission with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass sample, September 6, 2026.

This book's own sibling modules never call the trigeminal ganglion spinal: m58908 (Section 21.3, HSV-1 latency) describes it as "residing in the trigeminal nerve ganglia" with no spinal claim, m58940 (CNS infections) treats the trigeminal nerve as a distinct non-spinal cranial route into the CNS, and m58914 (varicella-zoster) correctly confines "the spine" language to VZV's actual dorsal ganglia. The Tick Tips Micro Connection box's anatomy sentence reads "Adult ticks have eight legs and two body segments, the cephalothorax and the head," printed exactly as quoted. A cephalothorax is by definition a fused head-and-thorax tagma, so naming "the cephalothorax and the head" as two separate segments is internally contradictory, and ticks (order Ixodida, class Arachnida) do not have a cephalothorax at all -- their two body regions are the capitulum (gnathosoma, bearing the mouthparts) and the idiosoma (bearing the leg pairs and housing the digestive/reproductive organs), unlike spiders and other arachnids, which do have a true cephalothorax plus abdomen. This book is silent on tick anatomy terminology elsewhere, so external references were used to confirm the correction: WikiVet, "Tick Morphology" ("Ticks have two body regions: a very large idiosoma... and a much smaller anterior gnathosoma (also called the capitulum)"), and Medicine LibreTexts, "10.2: General anatomy of ticks" ("Tagmatization in acarines is reduced to two unique tagmata with no distinction between the more conventional cephalothorax and abdomen"). The page's Tick Tips box reads "Adult ticks have eight legs and two body regions, the capitulum, which bears the mouthparts, and the idiosoma" with a visible Source note beside the correction (erratum 765), on the same footing as chapter 23's and 24's visible-Source-note corrections (errata 719-721, 751, 766). No item, hint, or key term on the page was built on the old wording. Found by the chapter 25 prose claim pass, September 14, 2026.

The HIV subsection's opening sentence (para fs-id1167663742703) reads "Human T-lymphotropic viruses (HTLV), also called human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV) are retroviruses that are the causative agent of acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)," presenting HTLV and HIV as alternate names for the same virus. They are distinct human retroviruses in family Retroviridae, subfamily Orthoretrovirinae, but different genera -- HTLV-1/HTLV-2 in genus Deltaretrovirus, HIV-1/HIV-2 in genus Lentivirus -- with different replication strategies (deltaretroviruses replicate chiefly by driving infected-cell division; lentiviruses like HIV replicate mainly by producing progeny virions) and different disease associations (HTLV causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and HAM/TSP, not AIDS). This book is silent on HTLV elsewhere -- no sibling module names it, so the false equivalence is not internally self-contradicted -- but it is a citable factual error: ICTV Retroviridae taxonomy (https://ictv.global/report/chapter/retroviridae/taxonomy/retroviridae) places Deltaretrovirus and Lentivirus as distinct genera of subfamily Orthoretrovirinae, and PMC9505669 describes their divergent replication biology.
